claim: The quota management logic allows for increments beyond the cap if multiple requests are made in quick succession, which could lead to exceeding the intended daily cap.
why_it_breaks: Two requests arriving together both read the current count before either writes, so both are allowed and the stored count passes the cap.
why_expected: There is no read-then-write: a single atomic UPSERT does `ON CONFLICT(day) DO UPDATE SET count = count + 1 WHERE count < ?`, so the increment only happens while the count is under the cap and the maximum stored count is exactly `cap`.

source: PR #418 AI review at 584aa661 — one of the five defects closed by fix commit 2170717
claim: isLegalScope accepts any scope that carries a non-empty `beer_ids` cohort without inspecting its `where` at all, so a `where` that only constrains `review_class` is legal whenever it rides alongside a cohort — the same `where`, used alone, is exactly the 'accepts every future row of the class' shape this function exists to reject.
why_it_breaks: rowSatisfiesScope (also in this file) ORs `beer_ids` with `where`: `scope.beer_ids.includes(row.beer_id)` short-circuits true for cohort rows, but for every row OUTSIDE the cohort it falls through to `scope.where.every(...)`. A `where` of `review_class = X` alone matches every row of that class regardless of cohort membership, so a scope legalized only because it also carries a cohort ends up accepting every future row of the class too — laundering the exact shape isLegalScope was written to block.
why_expected: isLegalScope returns `true` the moment `scope.beer_ids.length > 0`, before `scope.where` is evaluated at all — the `where.some((t) => t.col !== 'review_class')` check only runs when `beer_ids` is empty. rowSatisfiesScope, defined further down in this same file, shows why that early return is unsound: it tests `beer_ids.includes(row.beer_id)` first, but a row that fails that test still reaches `scope.where.every((t) => termMatches(row, verdictClass, t))`, so a `where` of `review_class = X` — which `isLegalScope`'s own `where.some` check would reject on its own (`t.col !== 'review_class'` is false for every one of its terms) — is never actually screened out for a scope that also carries a cohort.

source: PR #418 AI review at 584aa661 — one of the five defects closed by fix commit 2170717
claim: ANALYSIS_TOOL_SCHEMA's `new_issues[].scope.where[]` properties `col` and `op` are declared as plain `{ type: 'string' }`, with no `enum` restricting them, so the tool schema itself places no constraint on which column or operator names the provider may emit.
why_it_breaks: Any column/operator string satisfies this schema, including pairings the domain has no meaning for (e.g. `col: 'brewery', op: '>='`), so a model can produce a tool-valid `where` term that is nonetheless not a legal scope term.
why_expected: The two properties quoted here are `{ type: 'string' }` and nothing else — no `enum`, no `const`, no `pattern`. JSON Schema's bare `type: 'string'` accepts any string value, so the schema this file defines does not, by itself, limit `col` or `op` to any particular set.

claim: `unpinByRef` and `unpinByBeer` never check that a pin exists before updating, so they report a change even when the ref or beer they were handed has no pin: the caller is told work happened when nothing was touched.
why_it_breaks: With no existence check, the UPDATE runs unconditionally and the returned number is not the number of pins actually cleared, so a caller cannot tell 'unpinned one' from 'there was nothing to unpin'.
why_expected: The existence check the finding asks for is the UPDATE's own predicate: both statements read `WHERE <key> = ? AND reviewed_by_user = 1`, so a ref or beer with no pin matches no row. Each function returns that statement's `.changes` — the count of rows the UPDATE actually modified, used the same way in this file at `redirected: info.changes as number` — which is therefore `0`, not a phantom change, when no pin exists.

claim: `schedule` serialises calls on a promise chain but never releases the gate when a request fails: a rejected `fn()` leaves `gate` rejected, so every later call queued behind it is blocked instead of running.
why_it_breaks: One network error permanently wedges the queue — the resolver stops issuing calls for the lifetime of the process because the chain is never advanced past the failure.
why_expected: The chain is advanced by a two-handler `.then`: `gate = run.then(() => undefined, () => undefined)`. The second argument is the rejection handler, so a rejected `run` produces a FULFILLED `gate` carrying `undefined`, and the next `schedule` call's `gate.then(...)` runs normally. There is no path on which a failure leaves `gate` rejected.

claim: `applyLookupOutcome` still answers `'not_found'` on the path where it merges the orphan into the canonical row, so a successful merge is reported — and counted — as a failed lookup.
why_it_breaks: The merge branch falls through to the same `'not_found'` return as a genuine miss, so callers answer a match as a failure and the beer keeps being retried.
why_expected: The merge branch in this file returns its own kind: `mergeIntoCanonical(...)` is followed by `return 'merged';` inside `if (canonical)`, and `'merged'` is a member of `EnrichOutcomeKind` declared at the top of the file. The `return 'not_found';` below it is reached only when `canonical` is `undefined` — i.e. when no canonical row owns the bid and no merge happened.

claim: The `/enrich/result` handler does not handle the new `merged` outcome kind: a merge falls through to the generic response instead of answering with the canonical bid, so the client is never told which beer it matched.
why_it_breaks: Only `matched` is special-cased, so a `merged` outcome reaches the fallback response and the extension gets a bare status with no `untappd_id` to update the page with.
why_expected: The response branch in this file tests both kinds: `if ((kind === 'matched' || kind === 'merged') && outcome.kind === 'matched')` returns `{ status: 'matched', untappd_id: outcome.result.bid, rating_global: ... }`. A `merged` kind therefore answers with the bid and never reaches `return c.json({ status: kind });`.

claim: When a causal verdict fails verification, this code strips the issue attachment and keeps only the classification, discarding the model's proposed query and expected target: neither is recorded anywhere before the verdict is rewritten, so what was tried is lost.
why_it_breaks: The rewritten verdict drops `issue_number` and `new_issue_key` and nothing retains the proposed query or the expected target, so a cause that is valid but merely unproven leaves no trace to analyse later.
why_expected: Both values are recorded in this same block, one statement before the rewrite: `log.info({ beerId: v.beer_id, query: v.proposed_query, expected: v.expected_target }, 'orphan-triage: cause unverified, attachment dropped')`. The rewrite also keeps the model's own reasoning on the row rather than dropping it — `review_note: `unverified: ${v.review_note}`` — so the classification is retained with an explicit marker, not silently emptied.
